cues.text: On April 28, 2001, at the parish church of St. Mary in Chirattakonam, in the Archdiocese of Trivandrum, India, Father Johnson Karnoor exposed the Blessed Sacrament for the community's annual Novena to St. Jude Thaddeus.

A few minutes into the adoration, he noticed three distinct marks on the consecrated Host, paused his own prayer, and invited the assembled faithful to see them as well before reposing the monstrance in the tabernacle.
Father Karnoor left for a nearby parish and did not return to open the tabernacle again until Saturday morning, May 5.
He found the Host bearing what he described as a clear human face—a likeness he and others compared to images of Christ crowned with thorns.
The day's Scripture reading happened to be the account of Christ appearing to the doubting Thomas, a coincidence the priest noted in his own written deposition.
Karnoor summoned a photographer to document the Host before departing to celebrate Mass at a nearby parish.
The photographs, developed roughly two hours later, showed the face growing progressively clearer with each successive image — a detail recorded in his formal account of the events.
Cyril Mar Baselios, then Archbishop of Trivandrum, addressed the event directly.
He wrote that for believers, what had been witnessed was "something that we have always believed," and that if the Lord was speaking through such a sign, it required a response from the faithful.
The monstrance containing the Host has remained in the parish church since.

Chirattakonam remains the only entry from India in the broader Eucharistic Miracles exhibition assembled by St. Carlo Acutis, a modest parish church in Kerala carrying a devotional distinction shared with only a small number of sites worldwide.

The account rests chiefly on the parish priest's own contemporaneous written deposition and the photographic record made within hours of the discovery, offered here as documented local testimony rather than a claim of formal papal recognition.
